Houthis complete control of Bab el-Mandeb; Brent above $107

Facts

  • Houthi forces have seized Perim (Mayun) Island, the port of Mokha, and the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands, giving them effective control of both sides of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, per NPR, NBC News and PBS.
  • Roughly 12% of global trade and about 7% of global petroleum supply normally transit the strait.
  • The group declared a naval blockade of Saudi shipping in the Red Sea on July 20. A Houthi attack on a cargo ship in the strait last month killed six — the first fatalities from Red Sea shipping attacks in over a year.
  • A Saudi oil pipeline struck in an attack is out of service; repairs are estimated at three to five weeks. Saudi Arabia had been routing exports through the Red Sea as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been targeting vessels.
  • Brent settled around $107.46 Tuesday. Trump has described the US naval response as a "wall of steel"; the Houthis dispute his characterization of the situation.

Left view

NPR and The Guardian frame this as the predictable cost of an open-ended war with Iran: the US has spent months striking Iranian assets and now faces a proxy that has taken territory rather than been degraded. The Christian Science Monitor's reporting emphasizes that naval escort operations protect ships but cannot dislodge a force holding the shoreline, and that there is no stated endgame. MSNBC commentary ties the gas price at the pump directly to the administration's escalation choices heading into the midterms.

Right view

Fox News and the New York Post argue the opposite causal story: years of accommodating Iran and treating the Houthis as a nuisance rather than a state-backed military let this happen, and the answer is heavier strikes, not withdrawal. The Free Press and National Review have pushed for re-designating and directly targeting Houthi leadership, and criticize the 2025 Oman-brokered ceasefire that shielded American ships but left Israeli-linked shipping exposed — which, they argue, taught the Houthis that attacks pay.

Watch for

Energy analysts cited by CNBC and CSIS say the near-term question is insurance: war-risk premiums for Red Sea transits are the mechanism that actually closes a strait, and a further spike pushes carriers back around the Cape, adding 10–14 days and cost to Asia–Europe freight. Watch Saudi export loadings and whether Riyadh restarts the damaged pipeline on schedule. A move above $110 Brent feeds straight into US pump prices with a two-to-three-week lag, which lands in late October — weeks before the midterms. Also watch whether the administration expands the naval mission, which would require either a new authorization fight or another executive-authority argument in Congress.

Sources: NPR NBC News PBS NewsHour The Hill CS Monitor CNBC

Supreme Court blocks Trump's mail-ballot rules for the midterms

Facts

  • The Supreme Court on Monday refused to lift a lower-court block on new USPS rules governing mail ballots, leaving existing procedures in place for the Nov. 3 midterms.
  • The rules, which followed a Trump executive order, would have required states to hand the Postal Service lists of voters' names and addresses and to use specific barcodes and envelope designs before ballots could be delivered.
  • The order was unsigned and three sentences long, saying the administration is unlikely to succeed on the merits. Justice Kavanaugh wrote separately that even if the rule might fall within USPS authority, applying it this cycle would be unlawful because election officials lack time to implement it.
  • Justices Alito and Thomas dissented. Justice Barrett joined the majority.
  • Trump called it a "big loss for Republicans, and America itself," and praised Alito and Thomas. Separately, the Court heard argument this week on whether states may count mail ballots arriving after Election Day.

Left view

The Washington Post and NPR report this as a guardrail holding: an attempt to rewrite ballot rules months before an election, through the Postal Service rather than Congress or the states, was stopped by a Court with a conservative majority. Democracy Now! and the Brennan Center-aligned commentary emphasize the voter-list handover, which they characterize as a federal database of mail voters assembled without statutory authority.

Right view

Fox News documented a real split on the right: populist commentators attacked Barrett personally — one called her the biggest judicial disappointment since Souter — while the Daily Caller and others reported the ruling straight as a timing loss rather than a merits loss, noting Kavanaugh explicitly left the door open for the rule in a later cycle. Election-integrity groups including the Honest Elections Project are focused on the separate late-arriving-ballot case, where conservatives think they have the better argument.

Watch for

The late-ballot case is the one with real consequences: a ruling that federal law requires receipt by Election Day would invalidate deadlines in roughly a dozen states and could decide close House races. Analysts expect a decision before November given the timing. Also watch whether the administration reissues a narrower rule for 2028, and whether the Barrett backlash shapes how the White House talks about the Court through the campaign.

Sources: Washington Post NPR CNBC Fox News Daily Caller CBS News

House kills Al Green's impeachment push, with 64 Democrats helping

Facts

  • The House voted 232–147 on Tuesday to table H.Res. 1486, Rep. Al Green's privileged resolution to impeach President Trump. Forty-seven members voted present.
  • Sixty-four Democrats joined Republicans to table, including the 47 voting present. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries voted present.
  • Green's articles centered on the killing of two US citizens by federal immigration officers earlier this year.
  • This is the latest in a series of privileged impeachment resolutions Green has forced to the floor this Congress; each has been tabled.

Left view

Axios reported the story primarily as a Democratic leadership problem — Jeffries and most of the caucus want the midterms fought on cost of living, not impeachment, and a floor vote that fails makes the party look divided. Progressive outlets including Mother Jones argue the underlying grievance is serious enough that leadership's procedural dodge is itself the story, and that the deaths at issue have not received a real congressional inquiry.

Right view

Just the News and the Washington Examiner led with the Democratic defections, framing the 64 votes as evidence that even Trump's opponents regard impeachment as theater. Republican members including Rep. Walberg issued statements calling the resolution a distraction from appropriations work. The broader right-leaning argument is that repeated failed impeachment votes cheapen the tool and help Trump.

Watch for

Practically nothing changes in the near term — the resolution is dead and leadership on both sides wants it to stay dead. The number to watch is whether Green files again before November, which would force vulnerable Democrats in swing districts into a second uncomfortable vote. The immigration-enforcement deaths remain live as a litigation and oversight matter regardless of the impeachment vehicle.

Sources: Axios Just the News Rep. Al Green House Republican Cloakroom

Judge blocks DHS limits on student, academic and journalist visas

Facts

  • US District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV in Massachusetts temporarily blocked a DHS rule capping the duration of several visa categories.
  • The rule would have capped F student visas and J exchange visas at four years, and cut I visas for foreign journalists — currently open-ended in practice — to a maximum of 240 days.
  • Saylor called the government's national-security justification "exceptionally weak" and said DHS gave no reasonable explanation for the journalist cap specifically.
  • The block is temporary while a suit by a coalition of educational organizations and unions proceeds.

Left view

The Guardian and Democracy Now! frame the journalist provision as press-freedom-adjacent: a 240-day cap makes it structurally impossible for foreign correspondents to cover a full US election cycle, which they argue is the point. Higher-education groups quoted by NPR emphasize the enrollment and research consequences — international students are a significant share of graduate STEM programs and of university revenue.

Right view

Right-leaning coverage of this one is thin so far, which is itself worth noting. The general immigration-restrictionist case, made at the Washington Examiner and by groups like the Center for Immigration Studies, is that open-ended visa durations invite overstays and that fixed terms with renewal are normal in most countries. There is also a recurring conservative complaint about single district judges issuing nationwide blocks on federal immigration rules — expect that procedural argument on appeal.

Watch for

An emergency appeal to the First Circuit is the near-certain next step, and this administration has shown a pattern of going to the Supreme Court's emergency docket quickly. Universities are already into the spring admissions cycle, so the practical question is whether the block holds through the application window. If the rule is eventually revived, the immediate effect falls on students already mid-program who would need to reapply.

Sources: Irish Times Editor & Publisher Democracy Now!

Markets & Economy

  • S&P 500: 7,585.73, −0.45%. Dow: 52,093.11, −328.09 pts (−0.63%). Nasdaq: 25,981.57, −0.78%. Sixth decline in seven sessions.
  • Rates: 10-year Treasury 5.00% after touching 5.04%, highest since 2007. Fed decision 2 p.m. ET today; futures price a 25bp hike at better than 90%.
  • Oil: Brent around $107.46, up sharply on the Bab el-Mandeb seizure and the damaged Saudi pipeline. Brent rose roughly 8% and WTI nearly 10% over the prior week.
  • Gas: AAA national average about $4.33/gal, up from $4.17 a week earlier and $4.15 on Sept. 4. Every state is higher than a year ago.
  • Inflation: CPI 3.4% y/y through July; PCE 3.7%. Both well above the Fed's 2% target, which is Warsh's stated reason for tightening.
  • Other: AI-related corporate debt issuance is the year's dominant supply story — $220B by one count, with full-year ecosystem estimates up to $570B. The BIS lists an AI capex bust among its top global stability risks.

Sports Watercooler

  • Golf: Europe took the Solheim Cup 15–13 over the US at Bernardus Golf in the Netherlands (Sept. 11–13) after the Americans led into Sunday singles. At the DP World Tour's BMW PGA Championship, Jon Rahm talked about LIV Golf's fight to stay viable. Next Ryder Cup isn't until Sept. 2027 at Adare Manor.
  • Tennis: Quiet stretch post-US Open. The Asian hardcourt swing picks up with ATP 250s in China Sept. 23–29, and the Laver Cup is in London Sept. 25–27. Points here matter mainly for the November ATP and WTA Finals races.
  • Squash: The QTerminals Qatar Classic runs in Doha Sept. 12–18. Paul Coll won the London Squash Classic earlier this month, beating Joel Makin 13–11, 11–7, 11–8 for his 28th PSA title; Amina Orfi took the women's draw. PSA's Aug–Dec calendar has 24 events across 14 countries.
  • WWE: Sami Zayn beat CM Punk on the Sept. 11 SmackDown to win the Undisputed WWE Title — the week's big one. On NXT Tuesday, Mason Rook won a triple threat over Tony D'Angelo and Saquon Shugars for the NXT Title No. 1 contendership. Raw was in Springfield, Mass. Monday.
  • Hockey: Camps open this week — Nashville today, most clubs Sept. 17. The preseason is a compressed eight-day, 65-game slate Sept. 19–26, the first under the new CBA's 84-game regular season. Gavin McKenna, the Leafs' No. 1 pick, is the camp story; Connor Bedard is out until November after July shoulder surgery. Regular season opens Sept. 29.
  • Soccer: Arsenal stayed perfect in the Premier League with a 2–0 win over Sunderland, while Liverpool, Chelsea and Tottenham all dropped points. Forest beat Villa 2–1, leaving Emery still winless. No Champions League this week — the league phase resumes Oct. 13 after the opening round Sept. 8–10.
  • Football: Week 1 was the highest-scoring opening Sunday in NFL history at 53.3 points per game. Chicago hung 59 on Carolina, with Caleb Williams posting a line no Bear had before. The Giants beat Dallas 28–20, Arizona snapped a nine-game skid, and the Chiefs handled Denver 31–10 on Monday night. Week 2 starts Thursday; Giants–Rams on Monday.

item.title: Tue Sep 15, 2026 — 10-year Treasury hits 5% as the Fed opens a meeting markets expect to end in a rate hike
item.description: 10-year Treasury hits 5% as the Fed opens a meeting markets expect to end in a rate hike · Trump rejects the AI industry's own call for a slowdown · Supreme Court blocks Trump's mail-ballot rules for the midterms · EPA repeals power plant climate rules — and moves to bar future ones
item.content:encoded:
The Big Stories Today

10-year Treasury hits 5% as the Fed opens a meeting markets expect to end in a rate hike

Facts

  • The 10-year Treasury yield touched 5.0% on Monday before easing back — its highest since October 2023, and a level otherwise unseen since 2007. It traded near 5.04% early Tuesday.
  • The FOMC's two-day meeting begins today, with the decision and Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference Wednesday afternoon. Futures put the odds of a 25bp hike around 90%. The target range has sat at 3.50%–3.75% since a divided 9–3 hold in July.
  • It would be the Fed's first increase since 2023. August CPI came in at +0.4% for the month and 3.4% year over year, with core at +0.3%; energy did most of the work. Goldman Sachs flipped its call from hold to hike after that print.
  • Stocks closed lower Monday on a chip selloff, and futures were down again Tuesday morning.
  • The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 6.76% last week, up from 6.15% at the start of the year.

Left view

NPR and CNN Business frame the yield move as the bill coming due for an energy shock the administration's Iran policy helped create — households face higher mortgage, auto and card costs for a war they didn't vote for. Commentators on the left also note the political trap: the Fed is being asked to raise rates into a midterm year, and the White House spent the past 18 months arguing rates should be lower.

Right view

The Wall Street Journal editorial page and Washington Times coverage put the emphasis on inflation being above target since the Biden years and argue Warsh's credibility depends on acting rather than talking. Analysts at CNBC framed the same point more bluntly: having warned about prices for months, a hold now would revive questions about who is actually setting Fed policy.

Watch for

The dot plot lands with the decision Wednesday and is the real signal — one hike or a series. Bloomberg reported strategist Brian Barrow, who called 5% early, expects the selloff to run further. If yields hold above 5%, expect knock-on pressure in mortgages, regional bank balance sheets and highly levered corporate credit, plus a stronger dollar that squeezes emerging-market borrowers. Watch also whether Trump attacks the decision publicly; he has pressured the Fed repeatedly.

Sources: CNBC CNN Business Bloomberg Washington Times Kiplinger

Trump rejects the AI industry's own call for a slowdown

Facts

  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a roughly 3,800-word essay Saturday arguing the race to build frontier AI needs to slow, with international coordination and new government rules, because safety work is falling behind capability.
  • OpenAI's Sam Altman said companies need to pace the frontier; Elon Musk said Amodei was right; Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis called the direction correct.
  • Trump rejected the idea on Truth Social Monday, writing that the only guardrail AI needs is a strong, smart president, and later warning against killing the golden goose. He compared the warnings to past climate alarm and called the push against AI data centers a conspiracy.
  • The Washington Post reported that Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have discussed creating a new joint AI safety body.
  • Congress is not moving quickly. A Republican proposal for a 10-year moratorium on state AI regulation remains live; Amodei has called that approach too blunt.

Left view

NPR and CNN frame this as the president siding with growth over catastrophic-risk warnings coming from the builders themselves — the unusual fact being that the people asking for brakes are the ones with the most to lose. Left-leaning commentary ties it to the departure of the US AI Safety Institute's head and argues the administration has hollowed out federal capacity to evaluate the models it is cheering on.

Right view

Fox News casts Trump as defending American competitiveness against China, on the logic that a US slowdown is a Chinese speedup. But the right is split: Reason argues the executives asking for international regulation could simply slow down on their own and don't need Washington to do it, and Townhall warns that federal rules would hand incumbents a government-protected moat. The libertarian critique and the nationalist one land in the same place — no new federal AI regime.

Watch for

Whether the voluntary safety body materializes with real commitments or stays a talking point; whether the state-preemption moratorium gets attached to a moving vehicle in Congress before the midterms; and whether AI capex sentiment cracks — Monday's chip selloff showed the debate now moves semiconductor prices, not just op-ed pages. Data-center siting fights at the state and local level are the near-term flashpoint.

Sources: CNBC Fox News NPR CNN Axios Reason Washington Post

Supreme Court blocks Trump's mail-ballot rules for the midterms

Facts

  • The Supreme Court on Monday declined to lift lower-court injunctions against Trump's March executive order directing the Postal Service to impose uniform ballot and envelope requirements in federal elections.
  • The order would also have required states to hand USPS lists of mail and absentee voters 60 days before Election Day, and would have let the Postal Service decline to deliver ballots that did not conform.
  • Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that applying the rule to the 2026 elections would be arbitrary and capricious, because state and local election officials lack time to implement it.
  • Roughly two dozen Democratic-led states sued in April; both cases went to the same federal judge in Boston, who enjoined the order. A second judge issued a separate block on Sept. 3.
  • The ruling is about timing for this cycle, not a final judgment on the order's legality. An earlier decision in August had let other parts of the order take effect.

Left view

NPR and CNN report it as a significant defeat for an effort that would have given the Postal Service unprecedented power to withhold millions of ballots, and note the practical relief for election administrators who have been planning under uncertainty since spring. Democratic state AGs are presenting it as proof the courts still function as a check.

Right view

Coverage on the right emphasizes that the Court ruled on timing and implementability, not on the merits of uniform federal ballot standards, and that the administration retains the parts of the order already cleared in August. Conservative election-integrity groups argue the underlying goal — consistent ballot handling across states — survives and returns after November.

Watch for

Election officials now finalize mail-ballot procedures under existing state law, which removes a major operational unknown roughly seven weeks out. The merits litigation continues and could reach the Court after the midterms. Expect the administration to look for narrower administrative routes at USPS in the meantime, and expect mail-ballot rules to remain a live campaign theme in close Senate races.

Sources: NPR CNN CNBC The Hill The Conversation

EPA repeals power plant climate rules — and moves to bar future ones

Facts

  • EPA announced Monday it is repealing the Biden-era greenhouse gas standards for coal- and gas-fired power plants, which required certain coal plants to cut emissions 90% by 2032 and new gas plants to offset most of theirs.
  • In a separate but linked action, the agency proposes to find that the Clean Air Act does not authorize EPA to regulate power-plant greenhouse gases for climate purposes at all — a step intended to constrain future administrations.
  • EPA estimates the rescission saves consumers $310 billion.
  • The Natural Resources Defense Council said within hours it will sue to block the repeal.

Left view

NPR and the Washington Post lead on the second action as the more consequential one: repealing a rule is ordinary policy reversal, but declaring the authority itself nonexistent is an attempt to take the question off the table permanently. Environmental groups dispute the $310 billion figure as counting compliance costs while ignoring health and climate damages.

Right view

The Daily Signal and allied outlets frame it as a legal correction — the agency conceding it exceeded statutory authority rather than making a policy choice — and tie it to electricity reliability and price, an argument with extra force while gas and power demand rise alongside AI data-center buildout. The savings estimate is presented as relief for ratepayers.

Watch for

Litigation is certain and the authority question is squarely aimed at the Supreme Court's major-questions line of cases; a ruling endorsing EPA's reading would outlast this administration. Near term, watch utility capital plans and coal retirement schedules, several of which were built around the 2032 deadline, and watch whether states with their own carbon rules move to fill the gap.

Sources: Washington Post NPR Daily Signal AP

Russian drone hits Warsaw-bound train two kilometers from Poland

Facts

  • A Russian strike drone hit the locomotive of a Warsaw-bound passenger train in Ukraine's Volyn region Sunday, about two kilometers from the Polish border near the Yahodyn crossing.
  • The train carried 206 passengers. There were no casualties; a monitoring team's advance warning is credited.
  • Passengers included EU security advisers and former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson. Former CIA Director David Petraeus was reportedly on another train at the station.
  • Polish authorities identified the weapons as jet-powered Geran-5 drones. Ukraine and Poland called the strike an escalation.
  • NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte pledged additional support for Kyiv. Allies committed €70 billion in military aid for 2026 at the Ankara summit and have pledged to match it in 2027; over $10 billion has flowed through PURL and US foreign military sales in the past year.

Left view

The Guardian and France 24 present the strike as deliberate signaling at a NATO border rather than a stray, pointing to the Yahodyn rail gateway's role as the main EU–Ukraine supply artery and to who was aboard. The argument is that incremental probing works unless allies make the cost explicit, and that European air defense commitments have lagged the rhetoric.

Right view

Right-leaning coverage is split. Hawks at National Review-style outlets read it as confirmation that Moscow escalates when it senses hesitancy and push for tighter Article 4 consultations. Restraint-minded outlets argue the near-miss is precisely why the US should press harder for a negotiated end rather than deepen exposure, and note that a strike with no casualties is being used to justify open-ended commitments.

Watch for

Whether Poland invokes Article 4 consultations again, and whether allies extend air-defense coverage over western Ukrainian rail corridors — a step that edges toward direct involvement. Insurance and freight rates on the Ukraine–EU rail route are the practical tell. Also watch for movement on the stalled US-brokered proposal that envoys carried between Moscow and Kyiv earlier this month.

Sources: France 24 Al Jazeera NATO AllSides

Pennsylvania measles outbreak nears 700 cases with a third death under review

Facts

  • Pennsylvania's health department confirmed 693 measles cases across 38 counties as of Monday, up from 624 a week earlier and 460 earlier in the outbreak.
  • More than 130 people have been hospitalized. The state has confirmed two measles-associated deaths this year; a third — an adult woman with underlying health problems — is under review. Two infants died last month of related complications.
  • Four vaccinated people have contracted the disease: three adults and one child. Two MMR doses are about 97% effective, and breakthrough cases are typically milder.
  • The department has run more than 100 pop-up vaccination clinics, including in churches, community centers and homes.

Left view

NPR and CNN tie the outbreak's size to falling MMR coverage and to federal messaging that has softened on vaccine recommendations, arguing that state health departments are absorbing the consequences of a national retreat. The breakthrough cases are presented carefully — evidence of how much virus is circulating, not of vaccine failure.

Right view

Right-leaning outlets have given the outbreak lighter coverage, focusing on local response and on the breakthrough infections as reason for candor about vaccine limits rather than mandates. Some argue the deaths involved people with serious underlying conditions and that the policy response should be targeted protection of the vulnerable, not broad restrictions. Mainstream and left coverage is clearly leading on this story.

Watch for

Whether the case curve bends after the vaccination push — measles has a roughly 10–14 day incubation, so this week's numbers reflect exposures from Labor Day weekend. Watch for spread into neighboring states, school exclusion policies as the academic year gets underway, and whether the third death is confirmed, which would make this Pennsylvania's deadliest measles year in decades.

Sources: PA Dept. of Health CNN NBC News ABC27

Saudi Arabia threatens a firm response to Houthi attacks as Gulf risk premium holds

Facts

  • Saudi Arabia warned it will react firmly to Yemen's Houthis after ballistic missile and drone attacks wounded 13 civilians in the kingdom's south.
  • Saudi Arabia shut a major crude pipeline after drone attacks — a route specifically built to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
  • Brent crude rose as much as 7.1% last week to $108, its highest settlement since May 19 and its biggest one-day move in six weeks. It has held above $108.
  • Iran's security chief Ali Larijani has ruled out negotiations with Washington until conditions are met; Trump said on Sept. 1 he is not trying to force Iran back to talks.
  • China's foreign ministry separately warned against a space arms race, urging Washington to stop expanding military capabilities in orbit.

Left view

The Guardian and NPR argue the strike-for-strike cycle has produced no diplomatic opening and a large economic bill, and that the administration's refusal to pursue talks leaves the conflict without an off-ramp. The Yemen front is presented as the predictable widening of a war framed at the outset as narrow.

Right view

Fox News and the Washington Examiner frame Saudi resolve as evidence that regional partners are carrying more of the burden, and treat Larijani's refusal as proof Tehran was never a serious negotiating partner. The counterargument from restraint-minded conservatives at outlets like The American Conservative is that energy prices are now an American domestic problem with a midterm attached.

Watch for

S&P Global's crude research head Jim Burkhard describes a market adjusting to unresolved conflict and persistent maritime risk rather than returning to calm. Watch whether Saudi retaliation hits Yemeni port infrastructure, which would tighten Bab al-Mandab further; whether the shut pipeline restarts; and diesel, which at a record $6.06 a gallon is the freight-cost channel that pushes energy inflation into everything else.

Sources: Times of Israel CNN Business NBC News RFE/RL Rigzone

Markets & Economy

  • S&P 500: closed Monday at 7,619.98, −0.48%. Dow: 52,421.20, −152.09 points or −0.29%. Nasdaq: 26,186.41, −0.56%. Futures were lower again early Tuesday (S&P −0.49%, Dow −0.66%, Nasdaq 100 −0.48%).
  • Rates: 10-year Treasury near 5.04%, highest since 2007 outside a brief 2023 touch. FOMC decision Wednesday 2:00 p.m. ET, Warsh presser at 2:30; ~90% odds of a 25bp hike off 3.50%–3.75%. Summary of Economic Projections and dot plot accompany the decision.
  • Oil: Brent holding above $108, highest since May, on Iran-war supply risk, a shut Saudi bypass pipeline and Bab al-Mandab disruption.
  • Gas: AAA national average about $4.31/gal as of Sept. 13, up from roughly $4.14 at the start of the month and about $3 before the war. Diesel at a record $6.06. California highest near $5.81; Indiana lowest near $3.45.
  • Other: August CPI +0.4% m/m, 3.4% y/y; core +0.3%. Fuel costs up 28% y/y, diesel +52%. 30-year fixed mortgage 6.76%, up from 6.15% in January. Chipmakers led Monday's decline as the AI-pace debate moved into the tape.

Sports Watercooler

  • Golf: Off week on the PGA Tour — the Biltmore Championship in Asheville runs Sept. 17–20. Presidents Cup rosters are set for Medinah No. 3, Sept. 24–27: Brandt Snedeker picked Jacob Bridgeman, Patrick Cantlay, Chris Gotterup, Jackson Koivun, Xander Schauffele and Justin Thomas to join qualifiers Scottie Scheffler, Cameron Young, Wyndham Clark, Russell Henley, Sam Burns and Collin Morikawa. Geoff Ogilvy took Corey Conners, Nico Echavarria, Sungjae Im, Ryo Hisatsune, Nick Taylor and Christiaan Bezuidenhout alongside Si Woo Kim, Hideki Matsuyama, Ryan Fox, Tom Kim, Min Woo Lee and Adam Scott. Koivun, Bridgeman and Gotterup are debutants.
  • Tennis: Post-US Open lull, but the calendar reloads fast — Davis Cup qualifiers Sept. 18–20 (14 nations for seven Finals spots, Finals in Bologna in November), Laver Cup in London Sept. 25–27, then Seoul, Singapore and the Billie Jean King Cup the week of Sept. 21, and the Chinese swing (Chengdu, Hangzhou) from Sept. 23.
  • Squash: The PSA stop in Doha is live through Sept. 18, following events in London, Tashkent, Hong Kong and Maspeth, New York earlier this month. Busiest stretch of the early season.
  • WWE: Raw ran Arena CDMX Monday — WWE's first televised Raw from Mexico City since the 2011 SuperShow. Roman Reigns retained the World Heavyweight Title over Penta in a 21-minute main event. Chad Gable beat Dragon Lee to keep the Intercontinental Title. Money in the Bank qualifiers went to Je'Von Evans (over Big Cass and Austin Theory) and Lola Vice, who won her Raw in-ring debut over Raquel Rodriguez and Kelani Jordan.
  • Hockey: Main NHL camps open mid-week — Winnipeg and Vancouver on Sept. 17. Preseason is a compressed eight-day, 65-game slate from Sept. 19–26, the first under the new CBA, which also scraps mandatory fitness testing and expands the regular season to 84 games. Opening night is Sept. 29 with an ESPN tripleheader.
  • Soccer: Champions League Matchday 2 is Tuesday and Wednesday. Matchday 1 highlights: Real Madrid 2–1 Inter, Barcelona 5–1 Feyenoord, Bayern 5–0 Bodø/Glimt, PSG 6–1 Slovan Bratislava, Liverpool 2–1 Atlético, Napoli 0–1 Arsenal, Man City 2–0 at Porto, Man United 4–0 Sabah, Aston Villa 3–2 at Club Brugge.
  • Football: Week 1 closed Monday night with Kansas City beating Denver 31–10. Week 2 opens Thursday; the Monday nighter is Giants at Rams, 8:15 p.m. ET on ESPN/ABC.

item.title: Mon Sep 14, 2026 — Hormuz reopening talks collapse before they start
item.description: Hormuz reopening talks collapse before they start · The Fed meets tomorrow with a rate hike on the table · Midterm season opens with gas prices as the central argument · Indonesian ferry capsizes in the Java Sea; 129 still missing
item.content:encoded:
The Big Stories Today

Hormuz reopening talks collapse before they start

Facts

  • Iranian and Gulf diplomats were due to meet in Salalah, Oman today to discuss an Omani plan for restoring regular tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Oman's foreign ministry said Sunday the meeting is postponed indefinitely, giving no new date.
  • Hormuz has been largely closed to commercial shipping since late February, when Iran blocked the waterway following US and Israeli strikes. Transits are running at their lowest level since May.
  • The Omani framework reportedly included voluntary payments to Tehran framed as navigation-safety and environmental fees — the sticking point for several Gulf capitals.
  • The US was not a party to the talks. CNN reports administration officials have told Gulf counterparts privately they want any future US–Iran channel focused on the nuclear file, not on the strait.
  • Brent settled near $104 Friday; WTI was around $102 early Monday, up roughly 21% in a month and about 50% since the war began.

Left view

NPR and Al Jazeera coverage frames the postponement as the predictable cost of a strategy with no diplomatic exit: seven months of strikes and tanker interdictions have not reopened the strait, and Washington's refusal to join the one negotiation actually aimed at reopening it undercuts the regional partners it says it is defending. The Guardian's line through this conflict has been that the economic damage lands on consumers worldwide while the stated objective — Iran's nuclear program — remains unresolved.

Right view

Fox News and Fox Business emphasize that the pressure campaign is working on Tehran's balance sheet — CENTCOM strikes near Kharg Island and Jask have crippled Iranian export revenue — and that paying Iran transit fees would reward the blockade. Trump has argued new overland pipeline routes across the region, including through Syria, will make the strait less decisive over time. The Dispatch and other conservative outlets have been less sanguine, questioning whether a squeeze with no defined endpoint is a strategy or a stalemate.

Watch for

Energy analysts quoted by Reuters and CNBC see Brent holding a $95–$115 range while the strait stays shut, with spikes on any new attack. Axios has flagged that Trump's claim that Hormuz no longer matters much will be tested in the next few weeks by tanker-tracking data. Watch Gulf sovereign wealth flows, marine insurance rates (already the practical constraint on transits), and whether Oman can reconvene the meeting before the Fed's decision Wednesday hardens the inflation picture.

Sources: CNN NPR Al Jazeera Fox Business Axios

The Fed meets tomorrow with a rate hike on the table

Facts

  • The FOMC convenes September 15–16. Futures put the odds of a 25-basis-point hike between roughly 66% and 83% depending on the day and the data print; the odds were near 49% a week ago.
  • The current target range is 3.50%–3.75%. The Fed has neither cut nor hiked in 2026. A hike would be the first since 2023.
  • Chair Kevin Warsh said at Jackson Hole that inflation remains above the 2% target and that prices are the committee's predominant focus. He has not ruled out a hike.
  • Economists are split with the market. In Bloomberg's September survey, only 13 of 48 respondents expected an increase this month; the majority saw a hold.
  • CNBC reported that the president, vice president, Treasury secretary and senior economic advisers have all publicly urged the Fed not to raise rates. Warsh says the pressure has had no effect on his decisions.

Left view

NPR and Vox-style commentary makes two points at once: the White House campaign against Warsh is a direct assault on central-bank independence and would be treated as a scandal under a Democratic administration — and separately, that the hawks may be wrong on the merits, because rate increases are a poor tool against a supply shock caused by a war the administration started. Raising borrowing costs, on this reading, taxes households twice.

Right view

The Wall Street Journal editorial board's long-running position is that credibility is the Fed's only real asset and that flinching under political pressure would cost more than a quarter point ever could. National Review and Reason writers have made the same argument from the other direction — that the honest fix is ending the war premium and deregulating supply, not asking the Fed to accommodate inflation the executive branch manufactured.

Watch for

Barclays economists told Bloomberg the AI capex boom is acting as a shock absorber, blunting the usual channel by which higher rates slow housing and construction — which means a hike may buy less disinflation than the model says. Futures already price roughly 4.1% by December and about 4.6% by September 2027. A surprise hold would likely steepen the curve and weaken the dollar; a hike lands seven weeks before the midterms and will be read politically no matter how it is explained.

Sources: Bloomberg CNBC PBS NewsHour Fortune Washington Post

Midterm season opens with gas prices as the central argument

Facts

  • Labor Day marked the unofficial start of the general election. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are up on November 3.
  • Trump told reporters last week that oil and gas prices will fall "right after" the midterms and predicted the Iran war would end soon afterward. CNBC reported the remarks the same day crude topped $100.
  • US News and CNN both noted the tension with internal planning: the White House has separately discussed scenarios in which the conflict runs past January 2029.
  • Generic-ballot averages have Democrats up roughly 5 to 7.6 points depending on the model and likely-voter screen. Trump's approval sits in the high 30s.
  • Democrats need a net gain of three seats for the House. Forecasters currently favor them there; the Senate map remains unsettled.
  • At the GOP midterm convention in Dallas, Trump said handing Democrats Congress would set the country back a decade.

Left view

The Washington Post and NPR treat the "prices fall after the election" line as the story: it concedes that the pain is policy-driven and timing-dependent, which is the opposite of the usual argument that presidents don't control gas prices. MSNBC and The Atlantic have argued that a $4.31 national average and a $6.20 diesel record are the kind of kitchen-table numbers that override every other issue in a midterm.

Right view

The Washington Times and Fox News frame the fall campaign around a choice rather than a price: confronting Iran was a decision Trump made and Democrats would not have, and voters who want the nuclear program stopped should accept the interim cost. National Review and The Free Press have been more willing to say the quiet part — that a high-30s approval and $4-plus gas is a difficult combination, and that generic-ballot leads of this size have historically translated into real House losses.

Watch for

Historically a D+5.4 generic ballot maps to a net gain of 15–30 House seats. The variables to track: whether pump prices peak before early voting begins in October, whether the Fed's decision this week reads as a recession signal, and whether any Hormuz breakthrough materializes in time to move the numbers. Political scientists caution that gas prices affect vote choice with a lag of several weeks, which cuts against the president's timeline.

Sources: CNBC NPR CNN Washington Times Silver Bulletin

Indonesian ferry capsizes in the Java Sea; 129 still missing

Facts

  • The Indonesian-flagged ferry Virgo Transport 8 sank early Sunday in the Java Sea while sailing from Surabaya, East Java, to Banjarmasin, South Kalimantan.
  • The vessel carried 243 people and 89 vehicles. The captain's last radio contact, around 2 a.m. local time, reported the ship listing.
  • As of Monday: six confirmed dead, 107 rescued, 129 to 130 unaccounted for.
  • Indonesia's search agency has deployed 17 ships and aircraft and roughly 622 personnel from the military, police and other agencies. Rough seas and high waves preceded the sinking.

Left view

The Guardian and NPR situate this in a pattern rather than an accident: Indonesia's inter-island ferry network is chronically overloaded and under-inspected, and repeated disasters — Bali in 2025, others before it — have produced inquiries without enforcement. The framing is regulatory failure and the cost of thin maritime safety budgets in an archipelago of 17,000 islands.

Right view

Coverage in right-leaning US outlets is thin on this story, which is itself worth noting. Where it appears, the emphasis is on the rescue operation and on questions of operator liability and manifest accuracy rather than on systemic regulation. Wire services — AP, Reuters, ABC — are carrying most of the reporting.

Watch for

Survival odds fall sharply after 48 hours in open water; the search will likely shift from rescue to recovery within days. Expect scrutiny of whether the actual passenger count exceeded the manifest — a recurring finding in Indonesian ferry inquiries — and of why the vessel sailed into forecast heavy weather. Jakarta has previously responded to disasters of this scale with temporary route suspensions.

Sources: NPR Al Jazeera ABC News / AP ABC (Australia)

OpenAI rules out a 2026 IPO as AI leaders call for a slowdown

Facts

  • Sam Altman told Fortune in an interview published Saturday that OpenAI will not go public this year, calling an IPO now an ill-advised move given the safety work outstanding. A listing had been discussed for 2026 at a potential trillion-dollar valuation; the timeline now slips toward 2027.
  • Altman said OpenAI has internally discussed pausing development as models reach new capability thresholds, to let safety work catch up.
  • CNBC reported that Anthropic's Dario Amodei has proposed a plan to slow the pace of advancing AI capabilities, a position Altman and Elon Musk have both since echoed.
  • Separately, Layoffs.fyi counted 128,536 tech workers cut across 299 companies through September 10 — already past all of 2025. Uber's roughly 3,300 corporate cuts, about 10% of that workforce, lead the September total of 6,300-plus in ten days, alongside PayPal, Apple, Oracle and Zomato.
  • Stanford's 2026 AI Index found employment among software developers aged 22–25 down nearly 20% since 2024.

Left view

The Atlantic and Vox have argued that voluntary slowdowns announced by the companies that set the pace are governance theater — the same firms are simultaneously cutting entry-level staff and reinvesting in capacity. Mother Jones and labor-focused coverage put the emphasis on the 128,000 figure: whatever the stated cause, the displacement is real and the policy response is absent.

Right view

Reason and the Wall Street Journal editorial page have been skeptical of slowdown talk from a different angle, warning that safety framing becomes a moat: incumbents who call for a pause after building a lead are asking regulators to freeze the field. The Free Press and National Review have noted that Uber's restructuring is not, by the company's own account, an AI story — it is a reorganization to fund autonomous-driving competition, and conflating the two inflates the case for intervention.

Watch for

An OpenAI listing pushed to 2027 removes a major expected supply of equity from next year's IPO calendar and complicates valuation marks for private AI holdings — watch secondary-market pricing and SoftBank-style vehicles. On the labor side, the signal to track is whether entry-level technical hiring recovers in Q4 or whether the Gartner finding — that 22% of chief HR officers report a business leader halting junior hiring over automation — hardens into a structural change.

Sources: Fortune Axios CNBC Business Standard

Zelensky offers to meet Putin at the Miami G20; the Kremlin says no

Facts

  • In a Deutsche Welle interview released September 12, Zelensky said he would meet Putin at the G20 leaders' summit in Miami on December 14–15.
  • Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov rejected the idea, telling AFP that any face-to-face could only happen in Moscow. Presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said Russia has not decided whether Putin will attend at all.
  • The two have not met in person since before the February 2022 full-scale invasion.
  • Russian strikes killed nine people across Ukraine over the weekend, per RFE/RL.
  • Zelensky has said he plans to meet Trump in late September, as Washington pushes for renewed direct Moscow–Kyiv contact.

Left view

The Guardian and NPR read the offer as Zelensky maneuvering to keep Ukraine on an agenda that Iran and energy prices have crowded out, and the Kremlin's Moscow-only counter as a demand for symbolic capitulation rather than a serious condition. The concern in this framing is that a distracted Washington accepts a settlement Kyiv cannot live with.

Right view

The Wall Street Journal editorial board and National Review have argued that summits without leverage produce nothing, and that the answer is sustained materiel and sanctions rather than venue diplomacy. A separate strand on the right — the Trump-aligned position — treats any meeting as progress and pressure on both capitals as the point, with the Miami venue itself a deliverable.

Watch for

The Zelensky–Trump meeting expected in late September is the more consequential date; the G20 offer mostly sets up that conversation. Analysts also note the overlap with the Iran file: Russian crude is a direct beneficiary of the Hormuz closure, which reduces Moscow's incentive to settle while prices stay above $100. Watch European commitments at the next EU summit and whether Putin confirms G20 attendance at all.

Sources: RFE/RL Kyiv Independent Business Recorder / AFP

Markets & Economy

  • S&P 500: closed Friday at 7,656.98, up 0.86%. Dow: 52,573, up 509 points (0.98%). Nasdaq 100: up 0.9%. Friday snapped a four-session losing streak as oil and Treasury yields paused their climb.
  • Oil: WTI around $102.50 early Monday, up about 2.5% on the day and roughly 21% over the past month. Brent settled near $104 Friday and is up close to 50% since the war began in February.
  • Gas: AAA national average $4.313 per gallon as of September 13, up from $4.17 a week earlier. California highest near $5.81; Indiana lowest near $3.45. Diesel hit a record $6.20 average, squeezing trucking and agriculture.
  • Other: Fed funds futures price roughly 4.1% by December and about 4.6% by September 2027. Fed decision Wednesday afternoon. Watch marine insurance rates and Hormuz transit counts as the real-time read on the energy premium.

Sports Watercooler

  • Golf: Scottie Scheffler closed with a 66 at East Lake on August 30 to erase a three-shot deficit and take his second FedEx Cup — his 22nd PGA Tour win, and enough to move past Tiger Woods in career Tour earnings. The FedEx Cup Fall opens Thursday with the new Biltmore Championship at The Cliffs at Walnut Cove in Asheville; Procore is off the calendar this year.
  • Tennis: Alexander Zverev beat Ben Shelton 6-3, 7-6(2), 5-7, 6-2 in a three-and-a-half-hour US Open final Sunday for his second major and a $5.5 million check. Shelton, 23, was the breakout of the fortnight and the first Black man to reach a US Open final; the American men's drought in New York now runs past two decades. Elena Rybakina took the women's title over defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2.
  • Squash: Mostafa Asal holds a commanding No. 1 in the PSA world rankings (2,352 points) over Paul Coll (1,875) and Diego Elias (1,297) in the September 7 update. The Doha event runs through Thursday, with London, Ontario following September 15–19.
  • WWE: Sami Zayn is Undisputed WWE Champion again. On SmackDown from Mexico City Friday, Kevin Owens swung the title at Zayn, hit CM Punk instead, and Zayn finished it with a Helluva Kick — his second reign. Chelsea Green retained the Women's Title over Nia Jax. At Sunday Night's Main Event a week earlier in Atlanta, Trick Williams took the US Championship from Baron Corbin and Randy Orton beat Cody Rhodes.
  • Hockey: Camps open this week — Winnipeg and Vancouver on the 17th, St. Louis the 17th, Philadelphia with 46 players invited. Preseason starts Saturday the 19th: 65 games in eight days across 36 venues, a compressed slate under the new CBA. The regular season opens September 29 with an ESPN tripleheader, and it is the first 84-game season in league history.
  • Soccer: Manchester City won the derby 1-0 at Old Trafford on Sunday. Arsenal stayed perfect Saturday with a 2-0 over Sunderland; Liverpool were held 0-0 by Fulham at Anfield, Chelsea drew 2-2 with promoted Hull, and Spurs and Everton finished goalless. Nottingham Forest beat Aston Villa 2-1 and Ipswich edged Crystal Palace 3-2.
  • Football: NFL Week 1 Sunday. Carson Wentz came off the bench after Kyler Murray went out with a first-quarter concussion in his Minnesota debut and led the Vikings back past Green Bay. Baltimore handled Indianapolis 41-23, Jacksonville rolled Cleveland 34-10, and Las Vegas beat Miami 27-13. Monday night closes the week.

item.title: Sun Sep 13, 2026 — Trump says the Iran war ends "after the election" as Saudis press for strikes on the Houthis
item.description: Trump says the Iran war ends "after the election" as Saudis press for strikes on the Houthis · The Fed meets Wednesday and markets expect a rate hike — Warsh's first · BRICS adopts a New Delhi declaration built around routing trade off the dollar · Mail ballots are going out while the courts are still fighting over the USPS rule
item.content:encoded:
The Big Stories Today

Trump says the Iran war ends "after the election" as Saudis press for strikes on the Houthis

Facts

  • Speaking Saturday, Trump said the war with Iran — now in its seventh month — will end "very soon," and most likely just after the November 3 midterms. He said Tehran is stalling to complicate the election, and that he has no regrets about starting it.
  • Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has urged Trump to take direct military action against the Houthis, who on Friday seized Perim (Mayun) island at the mouth of the Bab el-Mandeb and now hold most of the Yemeni coastline along the strait.
  • Saudi Arabia's East–West pipeline remains shut after a drone strike Thursday in the Riyadh and Medina regions; Riyadh and Baghdad both say the drones came from Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate.
  • Gulf Cooperation Council diplomats are due to meet their Iranian counterpart in Oman on Monday on a temporary arrangement for Hormuz shipping. Iran says the strait stays closed until Washington meets terms from the lapsed June interim deal.
  • Reuters and Bloomberg report Riyadh is rerouting crude through the Suez Canal — longer and costlier for Asian buyers. WTI settled at $100.05 Friday, Brent at $104.61.

Left view

NPR and The Guardian frame the Houthi advance as the clearest evidence yet that a blockade-plus-sanctions strategy has not worked: seven months in, Iran has more leverage over global shipping than it did in February, not less. Vox and MSNBC focus on the election timing — the argument being that if the administration believes the war can be ended "immediately after" the midterms, it is fair to ask why it cannot be ended immediately before, and voters are paying $4.31 a gallon in the gap.

Right view

Fox News is leading with the Saudi request for US action and treating the Houthi gains as a case for escalating rather than folding. The National Interest argues the Perim seizure should force a rethink — that naval blockade without ground-denial has ceded a chokepoint to Tehran's proxy. The Free Press and Washington Examiner have pushed the harder line that a negotiated Hormuz arrangement now would ratify Iranian control of the waterway.

Watch for

Monday's Oman meeting is the near-term price signal: energy desks at Bloomberg and Reuters put a workable transit arrangement as worth roughly $8–12 off Brent, while a US strike on Houthi positions pushes it toward $115–120. Also watch whether Saudi's East–West pipeline restarts — it is the only meaningful route bypassing both chokepoints, and traders read its status as a proxy for Gulf export capacity. The White House has internally discussed the war lasting past January 2029, which is not the timeline Trump is offering publicly.

Sources: CNBC NPR Fox News NBC News National Interest CBC

The Fed meets Wednesday and markets expect a rate hike — Warsh's first

Facts

  • August CPI, released Friday, rose 0.4% on the month for a 3.4% annual rate, matching estimates. Core eased to 2.4%.
  • Gasoline did more than a third of the monthly damage, up 27.4% year over year; fuel oil was up 52%.
  • CME FedWatch put the odds of a quarter-point hike at roughly 90% after the print, up from about 70% the day before; Polymarket had it near 79%.
  • It would be the first hike of the cycle and the first policy move under Chair Kevin Warsh, who warned at Jackson Hole in late August that inflation remains too high.
  • The FOMC concludes Wednesday. Bank of America has penciled in three increases from here.

Left view

NPR and The Atlantic note that the inflation the Fed would be tightening into is largely an oil shock imported from a war the administration chose — squeezing households with higher borrowing costs on top of $4.31 gas, while core inflation is actually falling. Some economists quoted by CNBC go further, arguing there is no empirical basis for a hike and that Warsh is talking up inflation so he can claim credit when energy prices normalize.

Right view

The WSJ editorial board and National Review have backed Warsh's hawkishness as a credibility restoration after years of a Fed they see as behind the curve, and welcome his stated preference for a "quieter" central bank that does less signaling and less mission creep. Analysts cited by CNBC flagged that this posture puts the Fed at odds with a Treasury and a White House that want cheap money into an election.

Watch for

Whether Trump attacks the decision publicly — he has argued energy prices, not policy, are the inflation problem, and a hike three weeks before early voting is a political flashpoint. Rate-sensitive sectors (housing, regional banks, small caps) are the trade; the 2-year yield is the cleanest read on whether markets think Warsh is done after one. A hold instead of a hike would be a genuine surprise and likely a sharp equity rally.

Sources: CNBC CBS News BLS PBS NewsHour Kiplinger

BRICS adopts a New Delhi declaration built around routing trade off the dollar

Facts

  • The 18th BRICS summit ran September 12–13 in New Delhi. Modi said the 45-page New Delhi Declaration was adopted unanimously.
  • The declaration commits members to expand trade settled in their own national currencies and to link domestic payment and messaging systems — India's UPI, China's CIPS, Russia's SPFS — so transactions can clear outside SWIFT.
  • It condemned unilateral tariff and non-tariff measures as inconsistent with WTO rules, and warned about rising nuclear-confrontation risk.
  • Xi Jinping's first India visit in seven years. Putin, Iran's Pezeshkian, Ramaphosa, Prabowo, el-Sisi, Anwar, Abu Dhabi's MBZ and Abiy Ahmed also attended.
  • No common BRICS currency was endorsed; India has resisted that. Trump has threatened tariffs up to 100% on the bloc, which the White House says rests on executive-order authority.

Left view

The Guardian and Al Jazeera present this as the predictable cost of using the dollar and tariffs as coercive instruments: the more Washington weaponizes financial plumbing, the more countries build alternate plumbing. The Modi–Putin–Xi photo is read as a diplomatic failure for an administration that spent the year pressuring India on Russian oil and tariffs simultaneously.

Right view

The Wall Street Journal and The Dispatch are more measured, noting that interoperable national-currency settlement is not a reserve-currency challenge and that BRICS remains internally divided — India wants a US trade deal and has no interest in a Chinese-led monetary bloc. The Washington Examiner casts the summit as an authoritarian photo op given Iran's presence while it blockades a shipping lane, and supports the tariff threat as leverage.

Watch for

Whether Trump actually applies the 100% tariff and to whom — applying it to India would blow up a trade deal New Delhi is still seeking. Economists broadly expect BRICS Pay to matter at the margins first (Russia–India and Iran–China energy flows, sanctions evasion) rather than in dollar reserve share, which has moved slowly for a decade. Watch the rupee and the yuan's share of trade invoicing for the real signal, not the communiqué.

Sources: Al Jazeera New Delhi Declaration Business Standard Deccan Herald

Mail ballots are going out while the courts are still fighting over the USPS rule

Facts

  • USPS finalized its ballot-mail rule on August 26 under Executive Order 14399. It requires states to hand the federal government lists of every voter sent a mail or absentee ballot, and to use federally reviewed envelopes with unique barcodes. USPS says it will decline to deliver ballots in states that don't supply the list.
  • The Supreme Court in late August lifted a stay letting parts of the executive order proceed, but did not rule on the policy's legality.
  • On September 3 a federal appeals panel again refused to let USPS implement the plan. A district judge separately blocked it as ballots began going out.
  • DOJ has returned to the Supreme Court asking it to clear the way before November 3. Democratic-led states and voting-rights groups have filed a third round of challenges.
  • All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot.

Left view

The Washington Post and NPR emphasize the operational chaos: election officials are printing and mailing ballots under rules that may change by court order in October, and the deliver-or-not provision means a state's dispute with USPS could strand real voters' ballots. Votebeat's reporting stresses that the practical question is timing — even a government win may land too late to implement cleanly, which is its own risk.

Right view

Fox News and the House Oversight Republicans frame barcoded envelopes and voter lists as basic chain-of-custody — the kind of tracking already used for other accountable mail — and argue confidence in mail voting is low because it is the least auditable method. Thirteen Republican state attorneys general, led by Alabama, backed the rule in comments. The right's counter to the chaos argument: the litigation, not the rule, is what's late.

Watch for

A Supreme Court order on DOJ's application is the thing to watch, and the Purcell principle — the Court's reluctance to change election rules close to an election — cuts against implementation this cycle even if the government ultimately prevails on the merits. Election administrators are warning about ballot-return deadlines in states with tight receipt windows; expect litigation over individual rejected ballots in November regardless of how the rule fight ends.

Sources: NPR SCOTUSblog Federal Register Votebeat NBC News

Trump says he'd "love" to see a united Ireland, breaking decades of US neutrality

Facts

  • At his Irish golf course Saturday and in a meeting with Taoiseach Micheál Martin in Dublin, Trump said reunification of the Republic and Northern Ireland would be "fantastic" and that it will happen eventually.
  • US policy since the Good Friday Agreement has been deliberately neutral on Northern Ireland's constitutional future.
  • Sinn Féin's Mary Lou McDonald said the comments show the unity conversation has shifted and called on Dublin to start preparing.
  • UK Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch compared the remarks to Trump's talk about Canada and Greenland, calling them unhelpful loose talk.
  • New British PM Andy Burnham said weeks ago that a border poll is off the table.

Left view

The Guardian and PBS NewsHour report the substance carefully — that whatever one thinks of unity, an American president freelancing on another country's constitutional settlement removes a guardrail that has held for thirty years, and that the Good Friday framework depends on Washington being seen as an honest broker by both communities. Irish commentators on the nationalist side welcome it; unionist commentators read it as a threat.

Right view

The Daily Wire and NY Post are covering it largely as Trump being Trump — an offhand remark at a golf course, not a policy shift, and one that costs the US nothing. National Review has been more critical of this genre of comment, arguing that presidential asides about allies' borders have real diplomatic costs even when unserious, a line consistent with its position on the Canada and Greenland remarks.

Watch for

Whether the State Department walks it back. The mechanical constraint is unchanged: under the Good Friday Agreement, a border poll is the UK Northern Ireland Secretary's call and requires evidence a majority would vote for change — polling has not shown that. Watch Stormont's reaction this week and whether the DUP uses it to harden its position; analysts see little near-term market or policy effect, but it complicates the UK–US relationship at a moment when Burnham is new in the job.

Sources: PBS NewsHour The Hill Daily Wire AP via Spokesman-Review

A year after Charlie Kirk's assassination, the fight is over what followed it

Facts

  • September 10 marked one year since Kirk, 31, was shot and killed at Utah Valley University in Orem while speaking on a Turning Point USA campus tour.
  • Tyler Robinson, 22, faces aggravated murder charges. A judge ruled weeks before the anniversary that the case can proceed as a capital trial.
  • In the year since, employees at airlines, universities and media companies were fired or suspended over posts about the killing; NPR has tracked a wave of resulting lawsuits, and at least one arrest over an online post.
  • Vice President Vance urged listeners to contact employers of people celebrating the killing; Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy publicly pressed airlines to fire rather than suspend.
  • Reporting this week describes a durable pattern of neighbor-on-neighbor doxing that outlasted the immediate aftermath.

Left view

NPR and The Atlantic focus on the speech-retaliation machinery the killing set in motion — cabinet officials pressuring private employers over employees' political speech is, in this framing, the government doing indirectly what the First Amendment forbids directly, and the resulting lawsuits are the test case. The Guardian adds that political violence in the US is not one-directional and that the year's response flattened that.

Right view

The Washington Times and Townhall mark the anniversary around Kirk's legacy and Turning Point's growth, and argue the left never reckoned with the celebration that followed his murder. Breitbart is running the sharpest version, cataloguing anniversary commentary it reads as continued contempt. The Free Press and National Review have taken the harder internal line — that conservatives who cheered firings cannot now claim the free-speech mantle.

Watch for

Robinson's capital trial is the next real news event and will re-run all of this at higher volume; legal analysts expect pretrial motions over venue and the death-penalty notice into next year. The wrongful-termination and First Amendment retaliation suits NPR has tracked are the ones with precedential stakes — a ruling that official jawboning of employers is state action would reach well beyond this case.

Sources: NPR WFAA/TEGNA Washington Times Britannica

August tied the hottest month ever recorded as El Niño strengthens early

Facts

  • Copernicus reports August 2026 tied July 2023 as the warmest month on record globally, at about 1.65°C above the preindustrial average.
  • It was the first month since November 2025 to exceed 1.5°C.
  • Average sea surface temperature outside the polar oceans hit a record high; central and eastern tropical Pacific waters saw record warmth and severe marine heat waves.
  • Western Europe recorded its warmest summer on record, passing 2003.
  • Scientists attribute the spike to continued fossil-fuel warming plus an El Niño that intensified faster and earlier in the year than is typical.

Left view

The Guardian and Scientific American connect the record to policy: the US is seven months into an oil-price shock that has made fossil production politically untouchable, and climate spending has been deprioritized. UN officials quoted by UN News frame 1.5°C breaches becoming routine as the headline, not the tie for hottest month.

Right view

Reason and the WSJ editorial board typically emphasize the El Niño component — that a strong, early El Niño mechanically lifts global mean temperature and that single-month records overstate the trend signal. The broader right-of-center argument this year has been that energy security comes first while a war constrains supply, and that adaptation spending outperforms emissions targets on cost.

Watch for

Forecasters expect this El Niño to peak in late 2026, which historically means the following calendar year runs hotter still — 2027 is the year to watch for an annual record. Nearer term, record Atlantic and Pacific sea surface temperatures raise late-season hurricane and typhoon intensity risk, which reinsurers price through the fourth quarter. Watch European gas and power markets if a warm autumn follows the record summer.

Sources: Copernicus Scientific American UN News CBC

Markets & Economy

  • S&P 500: 7,656.98, +0.86% Friday, but −0.8% on the week. Dow: 52,573.29, +509.19 (+0.98%) Friday, −1.6% on the week. Nasdaq: 26,333.04, +0.96% Friday, −0.7% on the week — its first down week in three.
  • Oil: WTI settled at $100.05, down 2.4% Friday; Brent $104.61, down 2.8%. Both pulled back on news of Monday's Iran–GCC talks in Oman, but crude is still up more than 18% in September.
  • Gas: AAA national average $4.31, up 13 cents in a week and about 16 cents in nine days. Gasoline is up 27.4% year over year and did more than a third of August's CPI increase.
  • Other: Friday's rally snapped a four-session losing streak. Rate-hike odds for Wednesday's FOMC sit near 90% after the 3.4% CPI print, with core at 2.4%. Watch the 2-year yield for whether markets think one hike is the whole story.

Sports Watercooler

  • Golf: Quiet week before the Presidents Cup at Medinah, September 24–27 — Brandt Snedeker captains the US against Geoff Ogilvy's International side, with Scottie Scheffler leading the points standings. The Biltmore Championship at Walnut Cove tees off Thursday. Trump spent Saturday at his Irish course, where the Ireland comments happened.
  • Tennis: US Open men's final today: Alexander Zverev vs. Ben Shelton — the first Slam final this year without Alcaraz or Sinner. Shelton knocked out defending champ Alcaraz in a quarterfinal that ended at 3:33 a.m., the latest finish in tournament history, and is the first Black American man in a major final since MaliVai Washington in 1996. Elena Rybakina beat Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 for the women's title and her third major.
  • Squash: Mostafa Asal holds a commanding No. 1 on the PSA rankings (2,352 pts) over Paul Coll (1,875) and Diego Elias (1,297). The Doha event runs through Friday; London, Ontario starts Tuesday.
  • WWE: Sami Zayn beat CM Punk for the Undisputed WWE Title on Friday's SmackDown — a genuine upset finish. Raw is live Monday from Arena CDMX in Mexico City with Roman Reigns defending the World Heavyweight Championship against Penta. Worlds Collide is September 26.
  • Hockey: Most veteran camps open Thursday, September 17 (Penguins, Blues, Flyers all confirmed), preseason games start the 19th, and the regular season opens Tuesday, September 29 with an ESPN tripleheader. First year of an 84-game schedule, which has teams talking about depth and load management from day one.
  • Soccer: Champions League league phase opened September 8 and runs eight matchdays to January 27. Premier League played through the weekend, with Sunderland hosting Arsenal on Saturday night.
  • Football: NFL Week 2 Sunday — Bears at Panthers and Buccaneers at Bengals in the 1:00 window, Cowboys at Giants on Sunday Night Football. Monday nightcap follows.

item.title: Sat Sep 12, 2026 — Houthis seize Perim Island, completing their grip on the Bab al-Mandab
item.description: Houthis seize Perim Island, completing their grip on the Bab al-Mandab · Inflation runs at 3.4% as a divided Fed heads into Wednesday's decision · Trump's $5,000 "dividend" splits his own party as the GOP convention closes · Federal deficit hits $1.97 trillion with one month left in the fiscal year
item.content:encoded:
The Big Stories Today

Houthis seize Perim Island, completing their grip on the Bab al-Mandab

Facts

  • Houthi forces took Perim Island in the middle of the Bab al-Mandab Strait on Friday, a day after capturing the Red Sea port city of Mocha. Pro-government Yemeni forces withdrew rather than fight.
  • The group now holds effectively the entire Yemeni Red Sea coastline overlooking a strait through which roughly 12% of global trade passes.
  • Brent jumped more than 7% intraday on the news before settling near $104; WTI ended around $100 after touching $104. Both had topped $100 earlier in the week.
  • The IEA said Saudi crude output fell 2.3 million barrels a day in August to about 6 million — the lowest in more than three decades. Saudi flows through the strait have dropped from roughly 3 million bpd to about 400,000.
  • Strikes also shut a key Saudi pipeline. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has asked President Trump directly for US military action against the Houthis; the White House has so far offered intelligence and targeting help rather than strikes, keeping its focus on Iran and Hormuz.

Left view

NPR and NBC News frame this as the predictable cost of a war with no defined endpoint: seven months in, Iran's proxies have opened a second chokepoint rather than being deterred, and the administration is now fielding allied requests for a third front it has no plan to fight. The Guardian's line of criticism — a Middle East conflict entered without an exit strategy, at roughly a billion dollars a day — is being applied directly here.

Right view

Fox News and Al Majalla argue the opposite lesson: that a Houthi takeover of the strait "cannot be tolerated," and that hesitancy is what invited it. The complaint on the right is about tempo — that Riyadh reportedly did not get a green light for a large-scale air campaign in time to save Mocha, and that half-measures at Bab al-Mandab are what let Iran gain maritime leverage on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula.

Watch for

Analysts at the International Crisis Group and The Hill flag mines, short-range weapons and boarding operations from Perim as the near-term threat — the shift is from harassment to territorial control, which is much harder to reverse. Energy desks see the risk skewed upward: EIA's official second-half forecast of about $90 Brent now looks stale, and technical analysts are penciling ranges well above current levels if traffic stops entirely. Watch war-risk insurance rates, whether Saudi Arabia acts unilaterally, and the Oman meeting Iran says it will host with Gulf states on Hormuz shipping.

Sources: NPR NBC News CNBC The Hill Al Majalla Crisis Group

Inflation runs at 3.4% as a divided Fed heads into Wednesday's decision

Facts

  • August CPI rose 0.4% on the month, putting the annual rate at 3.4%. Core rose 0.3%, one-tenth above forecast, with the core annual rate at 2.4%.
  • The fed funds rate has sat at 3.50%–3.75% for all of 2026. The FOMC held in July on a 9–3 vote, with the three dissents favoring a hike.
  • Traders raised the odds of a quarter-point hike at the September 16 meeting after the report; CME FedWatch pricing has run in the mid-50s to mid-60s percent range. Nationwide now expects a hike.
  • Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said at Jackson Hole on August 28 that the central bank still has work to do on inflation and signaled readiness to act. Governor Christopher Waller had said he could accept a hold if CPI showed cooling.
  • Markets read the print as roughly in line and rallied: the S&P 500 snapped a four-session slide on Friday.

Left view

MSNBC's MaddowBlog and CNN tie the inflation problem back to the war rather than to Fed policy: energy is doing the work, households are absorbing it, and the president has said relief won't come until after the midterms. The argument is that a rate hike punishes workers for a supply shock the administration created, and that the Fed shouldn't be the only institution asked to clean it up.

Right view

The Wall Street Journal editorial page and Kiplinger's read of the data emphasize credibility: after leaving rates unchanged in July while inflation drifted above target, the Fed risks looking unwilling to finish the job, and investor doubt on that score is itself inflationary. Warsh's Jackson Hole framing — that there is still work to do — is treated on the right as overdue candor rather than hawkishness.

Watch for

Wednesday's vote and the dot plot are the whole story. A hike into a supply shock would be unusual and would sharpen the stagflation debate; a hold would likely be read as the Fed blinking. Either way, watch the dissent count — three dissents in July was already unusual, and a similarly split vote would tell you the committee has no consensus about what an energy-driven price spike requires. Mortgage rates and the 2-year yield will move first.

Sources: CNBC BLS Kiplinger Chase Schwab

Trump's $5,000 "dividend" splits his own party as the GOP convention closes

Facts

  • Republicans wrapped their first-ever midterm convention in Dallas on Thursday night. JD Vance spoke, followed by Trump, who urged Americans to vote Republican.
  • Trump pledged a $5,000 "Trump dividend" to every adult citizen — conditional on Republicans holding both the House and Senate in November.
  • The cost would run past $1 trillion. Congress would have to appropriate it, and the GOP's House majority is razor-thin.
  • Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said the payments would add to debt and inflation. Fox's Laura Ingraham pressed Trump on whether it amounts to a bribe. Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) said flatly it isn't happening.
  • Early convention nights drew rows of empty seats at the American Airlines Center, with last-minute efforts to fill them.

Left view

NPR and The New Republic cover the pledge as an admission that the affordability argument is landing: with a UMass Amherst poll showing Democrats ahead in both chambers and Republican unpopularity rooted in the cost of food, fuel and health care, the response is a one-time check rather than a policy. The conditional framing — money only if you vote a certain way — is the part Democrats are amplifying.

Right view

This is where the interesting fight is, because the sharpest criticism is conservative. National Review's Charles C.W. Cooke called the idea catastrophic morally, practically and politically. The Washington Examiner editorial board ran "Against Trump's $5,000 bribe," arguing it would widen deficits, raise inflation and worsen the affordability squeeze it's meant to fix. Former Sen. Pat Toomey was blunter still, and some on the right are calling it a first step toward universal basic income.

Watch for

Whether any appropriations vehicle materializes — nobody expects one before November. The more consequential question is the fiscal-hawk split the pledge exposed: the same week Treasury reported a $1.97 trillion deficit, the party's own editorial pages broke with its leader over a trillion-dollar giveaway. Watch whether House fiscal hawks put that objection on the record, and whether the dividend shows up in GOP candidates' own ads or quietly doesn't.

Sources: NPR The Hill Washington Examiner Newsweek Washington Examiner

Federal deficit hits $1.97 trillion with one month left in the fiscal year

Facts

  • Treasury reported Friday that the deficit for the first 11 months of fiscal 2026 reached $1.97 trillion — already above the full-year fiscal 2025 gap of $1.775 trillion.
  • August's monthly shortfall was $166.8 billion, flattered by calendar timing: because August 1 fell on a Saturday, Medicare and Social Security payments went out in July instead.
  • Adjusting for those calendar shifts, the 11-month deficit is down about 5% from the same stretch of 2025.
  • Spending ran $6.81 trillion and revenue $4.85 trillion, each up about 3% on an adjusted basis. Interest costs hit a record — roughly $1.4 trillion.
  • September is often a surplus month because of corporate tax deadlines, so the final figure should land below the current running total's trajectory.

Left view

Center-left coverage at Bloomberg and Reuters focuses on composition rather than the headline: revenue growth is keeping pace with spending growth, so the gap is driven substantially by interest on debt accumulated under tax cuts, plus war costs. The implied argument is that the deficit is a revenue choice, not evidence that social spending is out of control.

Right view

The Epoch Times and the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (nonpartisan but a favorite citation on the right) treat $1.4 trillion in annual interest as the alarm bell — debt service now rivals the largest line items in the budget, crowding out everything else and leaving the country exposed if bond markets demand higher yields. It's the same fiscal-hawk argument now being turned against the president's own dividend proposal.

Watch for

The final fiscal-year number in mid-October, and the 10-year Treasury yield in the meantime — rising yields make the interest line compound faster. Bloomberg notes the debt burden is heading within a few years toward levels unseen in US history. Also watch how the deficit figure gets used in the September appropriations fight, where both parties have an incentive to cite it selectively.

Sources: Bloomberg Reuters CRFB Spokesman-Review

EU frees €6.1 billion for Ukraine, clearing the way for Patriot interceptors

Facts

  • The European Commission formally approved a €6.1 billion (about $7.1 billion) tranche on Friday for Ukrainian defense procurement.
  • The money covers air and missile defense, ammunition, drones and electronic warfare, and comes out of the EU's €90 billion support loan.
  • Crucially, the approval includes exemptions letting Kyiv buy US-made PAC-3 interceptors — among the few munitions capable of stopping Russian ballistic missiles.
  • Defence and Space Commissioner Andrius Kubilius announced the decision in Brussels; member states had signed off earlier in the week.
  • Ukraine has put its 2026 defense needs at roughly $120 billion.

Left view

The Guardian and European outlets present this as Europe doing what it said it would — converting a headline loan figure into actual interceptors on a timeline that matters, and specifically working around procurement rules to buy American systems Kyiv needs rather than waiting for European production to scale.

Right view

Coverage on the right splits. The Wall Street Journal editorial line has generally welcomed European money going to American defense manufacturers as burden-sharing that finally works. Restraint-minded outlets such as Reason remain skeptical of open-ended European and American commitments, especially with US attention and munitions stockpiles already stretched by the Iran war.

Watch for

Delivery timelines, not announcements.
